vignette:
The Weight of Invisible Things

Maria is a fifty-seven-year-old Latina detective with nearly three decades on the force. She carries herself with the kind of quiet authority that comes from years of walking into rooms no one else wants to enter. She has solved homicides, worked narcotics, survived a difficult divorce, and raised two sons largely on her own. She has always believed, with some pride, that she is not the kind of person who falls apart.

Four years ago, that belief was tested in a way she could not have anticipated.

Maria was first on scene at a warehouse in the industrial district, responding to a report of an unconscious worker. The building housed a chemical storage operation, and something had gone badly wrong. She entered without full protective gear - the call had come in as a medical emergency, not a hazmat situation - and spent nearly twenty minutes inside before anyone understood what was leaking. She remembers the smell first: sweet, almost floral, wrong in a way she couldn't name. Then the burning in her throat. Then the sensation that the air itself had turned against her. By the time the hazmat team arrived and pulled her out, two of her colleagues were vomiting on the pavement and Maria could not stop her hands from shaking.

She was hospitalized for three days. The doctors used words like "acute toxic exposure" and "pulmonary irritation" and told her she was lucky. She went back to work in two weeks because that is what she does.

But something did not go back with her.

Now, Maria wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart hammering, certain she can smell something chemical in the air of her apartment. She gets up, checks the stove, opens windows, sometimes stands on her small balcony breathing deliberately until the feeling passes. She has had her building's ventilation system inspected twice. Both times, nothing was found. She knows this. It does not help.

At work, she avoids the evidence room when certain types of seized substances are being logged. She takes the long route around the building to bypass the cleaning supply closet, and she has never told anyone why. When a case recently brought her back to the industrial district, she sat in her car for eleven minutes before she could open the door. She did eventually open it. She always does. But the cost is higher than it used to be.

She describes herself as "jumpy in a way that doesn't make sense." Loud, sudden sounds - a car backfiring, a door slamming - send a jolt through her body that takes minutes to subside. She has trouble concentrating during briefings and finds herself reading the same paragraph of a case report three or four times. Her sergeant has noticed she is slower to volunteer for certain assignments, though he has attributed it to her age.

Maria does not correct him.

She has grown more isolated since the exposure. She and her ex-husband were already long divorced, but she has pulled back from her sons as well, deflecting their calls, keeping visits short. She tells herself she is protecting them from her bad moods. What she cannot quite articulate is that being around people she loves makes her feel strangely fragile, as though she is holding something breakable that she might drop.

She carries a persistent, low-grade sense that her body is no longer entirely trustworthy - that it was contaminated in some way that the hospital tests did not fully capture. She monitors herself for symptoms constantly. A cough, a headache, unusual fatigue: each one briefly confirms her fear before she talks herself down. She describes this as "waiting for the other shoe to drop."

What Maria finds most disorienting is not the nightmares or the hypervigilance, but the loss of the self she recognized. She was someone who walked into warehouses without hesitating. She is not sure where that woman went, or whether she is still findable.
